passage:
Honey has been used as a food and a medicine for thousands of years. Because it contains very little water and is naturally acidic, bacteria cannot easily grow in it. Sealed jars of honey found in ancient tombs were still edible when they were opened, which is why honey is often described as a food that never spoils.

Still, this reputation has limits. Honey absorbs moisture from the air, and once its water content rises, fermentation becomes possible. A jar left open in a humid kitchen will not last thousands of years. The preservation depends less on the honey itself than on how it is stored.
stem: According to the passage, why can bacteria not easily grow in honey?
options: It has little water and is acidic
It is stored in sealed jars
It was used as a medicine
It absorbs moisture from the air
solutionSteps: Locate the word 'bacteria' in the passage.
The sentence begins with 'Because', which directly signals the reason.
The reason given is low water content and natural acidity.

trapExplanations.1: Sealing preserved the tomb honey, but the passage attributes bacterial resistance to composition, not packaging.
trapExplanations.2: Medicinal use is background information, not a cause.
trapExplanations.3: This is what *undermines* preservation, stated in the second paragraph — the opposite role.

passage:
For most of the twentieth century, city planners treated traffic congestion as a problem of insufficient road capacity. The remedy seemed obvious: build more lanes. Yet a pattern repeated itself across dozens of cities. A widened highway would relieve congestion for a year or two, after which traffic would return to its former levels, and sometimes exceed them.

Economists eventually named the mechanism induced demand. Road space is not consumed by a fixed number of drivers; it is consumed by however many drivers find the journey worth making. Adding capacity lowers the effective cost of driving in time, which draws in trips that were previously not worth taking — journeys deferred, routes switched, or moves to more distant housing. The new lanes fill because they were built.

This does not mean road building is never justified. It means capacity cannot be evaluated in isolation from price. Where driving is charged closer to its true cost through tolls or parking fees, added capacity behaves far more like planners originally expected.
stem: According to the passage, why did widened highways fail to relieve congestion permanently?
options: Lower travel time attracted trips that had not previously been made
The new lanes were poorly designed
Populations grew faster than roads could be built
Drivers preferred older routes
solutionSteps: Locate the explanation: the second paragraph names the mechanism.
'Adding capacity lowers the effective cost of driving in time, which draws in trips that were previously not worth taking.'
That is induced demand — new trips, not merely existing ones.

trapExplanations.1: Design quality is never raised; the passage says the pattern repeated across dozens of cities.
trapExplanations.2: Population growth is a plausible real-world factor but is not the passage's explanation.
trapExplanations.3: The passage mentions route switching as part of induced demand, not a preference for old routes.

To restate the problem described in the first paragraph

options: In cities with widened highways, the total number of trips remained unchanged
Some widened highways cost more than planners expected
Congestion returned more slowly in smaller cities

passage:
The conventional account of the printing press credits it with spreading new ideas. The mechanism seems self-evident: cheaper books, wider circulation, faster diffusion. But historians of the period have increasingly argued that this account inverts the more important effect. What print changed first was not the spread of the new but the stabilisation of the old.

In a manuscript culture, every copy differed. Scribes corrected, abbreviated and silently emended, so that two copies of the same work might diverge substantially within a few generations. Print did not eliminate error, but it made error identical across thousands of copies, and therefore visible. A reader in one city could write to a reader in another and refer to the same passage on the same page. Discrepancy became detectable in a way it had never been.

The consequence was less dramatic than a revolution in ideas and more consequential: the emergence of a shared textual baseline against which claims could be checked. What looks in retrospect like the rapid spread of new theories may owe less to the volume of printed matter than to the fact that, for the first time, a disagreement could be located precisely.
stem: The writer's main claim about the printing press is that:
options: its most important effect was making texts uniform rather than spreading ideas
it did not significantly affect the circulation of books
it introduced more errors than manuscript copying did
it was less influential than historians once believed
solutionSteps: The first paragraph presents the conventional view, then reverses it: 'this account inverts the more important effect'.
The stated priority is 'the stabilisation of the old' over 'the spread of the new'.
The rest of the passage develops uniformity as the key consequence.

trapExplanations.1: The writer does not deny wider circulation; the claim is about which effect mattered most.
trapExplanations.2: The passage says print made errors identical and visible, not more numerous.
trapExplanations.3: The writer argues the press was highly consequential — just for a different reason. This is the strongest distractor because it sounds appropriately revisionist.

passage:
Bamboo is often called a tree, but it is in fact a grass. Some species grow more than half a metre in a single day, which makes bamboo one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth. Because a stem reaches its full height in months rather than decades, bamboo can be cut again and again from the same root system, which stays in the ground and sends up new growth.

This has made the plant attractive to builders looking for materials that renew quickly. Its stems are light and, for their weight, remarkably strong. Untreated bamboo, however, absorbs water and is readily attacked by insects, so it has to be treated before it can be used in construction. The plant's speed of growth is an advantage only once that problem has been dealt with.
stem: According to the passage, why is bamboo not really a tree?
options: It belongs to the grass family.
It grows far too quickly to be a tree.
It is cut without ever being replanted.
Its stems are light rather than woody.
solutionSteps: Find the sentence that makes the classification.
The first sentence states it directly: bamboo is a grass.
The other options are facts from the passage, but none is the reason for the classification.

trapExplanations.1: Speed of growth is mentioned, but it is not what decides the classification.
trapExplanations.2: Harvesting without replanting is a consequence of the root system, not a reason it is a grass.
trapExplanations.3: The passage calls the stems light and strong but never contrasts them with wood.

passage:
For most of the twentieth century, museums competed on the size of their collections. A great museum was one that owned a great many objects, and the measure of a new acquisition was largely whether it filled a gap on a shelf.

That assumption has weakened. Storage is expensive, and most collections are now so large that only a small part is ever shown; some institutions display less than five per cent of what they hold. Critics argue that objects locked away serve no public purpose, and would do more good if they were lent, shared or returned to the places they came from.

Defenders reply that a collection is a research resource rather than an exhibition. An object no visitor ever sees may still be studied, and the worth of a holding cannot be measured by how often it is put on a wall.
stem: How were museums traditionally judged, according to the passage?
options: By the number of objects they owned.
By the number of visitors they attracted.
By how much of their collection was on display.
By the quality of the research they produced.
solutionSteps: The first paragraph describes the older assumption.
'Competed on the size of their collections' and 'owned a great many objects' both point the same way.
Size of holdings was the measure.

trapExplanations.1: Visitor numbers are never mentioned in the passage.
trapExplanations.2: Display is raised later, as part of the criticism of the old view.
trapExplanations.3: Research appears only in the defenders' reply, not in the traditional measure.

passage:
For most of the twentieth century, museums competed on the size of their collections. A great museum was one that owned a great many objects, and the measure of a new acquisition was largely whether it filled a gap on a shelf.

That assumption has weakened. Storage is expensive, and most collections are now so large that only a small part is ever shown; some institutions display less than five per cent of what they hold. Critics argue that objects locked away serve no public purpose, and would do more good if they were lent, shared or returned to the places they came from.

Defenders reply that a collection is a research resource rather than an exhibition. An object no visitor ever sees may still be studied, and the worth of a holding cannot be measured by how often it is put on a wall.
stem: How do the defenders answer the criticism?
options: They argue a collection's value lies in research rather than display.
They deny that most objects remain in storage.
They claim storage is cheaper than the critics suggest.
They warn that objects on display are gradually damaged.
solutionSteps: The final paragraph gives the reply.
It reframes the collection as a research resource, not an exhibition.
An unseen object can still be studied.

trapExplanations.1: The defenders accept the storage figures; they dispute what follows from them.
trapExplanations.2: Cost is never contested in the reply.
trapExplanations.3: Damage from display is not raised anywhere in the passage.

passage:
It is often said that a scientific theory must be falsifiable: there must be some observation which, if it were made, would show the theory to be wrong. The appeal of the criterion is plain. It separates claims that risk something from claims that can absorb any evidence at all.

Applied strictly, however, the rule is harder to use than it looks. Theories are seldom tested on their own. A prediction follows not from the theory alone but from the theory together with assumptions about instruments, background conditions and auxiliary hypotheses, any of which might be blamed when the prediction fails. What a failed test refutes is a whole package, and deciding which part to discard is a matter of judgement rather than of logic.

None of this makes the criterion worthless. It remains a warning against claims built so that nothing could ever count against them. It is simply a blunter instrument than it first appears.
stem: What, according to the passage, is the appeal of falsifiability?
options: It separates claims that risk being wrong from claims that cannot be.
It identifies which scientific theories are true.
It removes the need for judgement in science.
It makes predictions easier to derive from a theory.
solutionSteps: The appeal is stated at the end of the first paragraph.
It divides claims that risk something from claims that absorb any evidence.
That is a distinction about testability, not about truth.

trapExplanations.1: Falsifiability concerns whether a theory could be shown false, not whether it is true.
trapExplanations.2: The passage argues the opposite: judgement turns out to be unavoidable.
trapExplanations.3: Deriving predictions is described as involving extra assumptions, not made easier.
